content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, a 'new name' symbolizes the new identity, character, and status God confers on a person He has redeemed and claimed as His own. It marks a decisive transformation of the person's nature and relationship to God — the old identity is replaced by a God-given one — and, eschatologically, it signifies the believer's full acceptance, ownership by God, and glorified identity in the age to come.", "primary_basis": ["Revelation 2:17 (a white stone with a new name written on it, known only to the one who receives it)", "Revelation 3:12 (Christ writes on the overcomer the name of God, the name of the New Jerusalem, and 'my new name')", "Isaiah 62:2 (Zion 'shall be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will give')", "Isaiah 65:15 (God's servants called 'by another name')", "Genesis 17:5 and 17:15 (Abram to Abraham; Sarai to Sarah)", "Genesis 32:28 (Jacob renamed Israel)", "John 1:42 and Matthew 16:17-18 (Simon renamed Cephas/Peter)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Personal intimacy with Christ: the new name of Revelation 2:17, known only to its recipient, signifies a unique, private relationship between the individual believer and God — an emphasis found widely in devotional and pastoral literature (e.g., strands going back to expositors like Charles Spurgeon and George MacDonald).", "basis": ["Revelation 2:17"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The 'new name' is Christ's own name (or God's name) placed upon believers, symbolizing His ownership of them and their belonging to Him and to the New Jerusalem, rather than a distinct personal name for each believer.", "basis": ["Revelation 3:12", "Revelation 14:1", "Revelation 22:4"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Corporate/covenantal restoration: in the Isaiah passages, the new name signifies the eschatological vindication and changed status of Zion/Israel (from 'Forsaken' and 'Desolate' to 'Hephzibah' and 'Beulah'), i.e., a national-covenantal renewal rather than individual conversion; Christian interpreters then apply this typologically to the church.", "basis": ["Isaiah 62:2-4", "Isaiah 62:12", "Hosea 1-2 (renaming of Hosea's children)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Historical-critical background reading: the white stone and name in Revelation 2:17 evoke Greco-Roman customs (a tessera of admission to a feast, an acquittal pebble in court, or an amulet bearing a secret divine name), so the symbol denotes admission, acquittal, or protective power rather than personal transformation per se.", "basis": ["Revelation 2:17 read against first-century cultural background (commentary literature, e.g., discussions in Aune, Beale, Hemer)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Sectarian/ritual reading: in Latter-day Saint temple practice, the 'new name' is a literal name given in ordinances, connected to exaltation — a materially different, ritualized interpretation outside mainstream Christian exegesis.", "basis": ["Revelation 2:17 as used in LDS teaching"], "prominence": "rare"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is a broadly recognizable consensus that 'new name' symbolizes God-given new identity/transformation and eschatological acceptance, anchored in the Old Testament renaming narratives (Abraham, Israel, Peter) and in Isaiah 62 and Revelation 2-3. The main interpretive disagreements concern details rather than the core symbol: whether the Revelation 2:17 name is the believer's own transformed identity, Christ's name conferred on the believer, or a token of admission/vindication; and whether the Isaiah texts are primarily corporate (Zion/Israel) or individually applied. These readings overlap and are often combined in commentaries, so the field is not sharply polarized."}
